title: Progressive and Continuous Tenses
keyIdea: The progressive (or continuous) form of a verb shows an action that is going on at a certain time. It uses a form of be plus the -ing word (the present participle). Present progressive: I am walking, she is walking, they are walking. Past progressive: I was walking, we were walking. Future progressive: I will be walking. Use the present progressive for what is going on now and the simple present for habits and facts (I eat lunch at noon). Use the past progressive for a long action that a quick event cut into: she was reading when the phone rang.
familyTip: At tea time, ask: what were you doing at 10 o'clock this morning? What will you be doing at 10 tomorrow? Listen for was or were + -ing and will be + -ing. Then swap: you ask, your child checks your verbs.

visual.caption: When is each action going on? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: drag the helper for each time on a timeline, spell -ing words, sort now from habit, build interrupted actions and fix verb slips.

kid: Some actions go on for a while. To show that, we use a helper and an ing word. I am reading. The helper is am. The ing word is reading.
The helper tells you when. Now: am, is or are. In the past: was or were. In the future: will be. At 3 pm yesterday, we were swimming. At 3 pm tomorrow, we will be swimming.
Now or every day? I am eating lunch means it is going on now. I eat lunch at noon means I do it every day. A habit has no helper and no ing.

Sometimes a quick thing cuts in. She was reading when the phone rang. The reading went on for a long time, so it gets was and ing. The ring was quick, so it is just rang. To spell the ing word, double the last letter of short words like run (running). Drop the e at the end of words like make (making).
adult: Ages 9 to 10. The progressive (continuous) form is be + the present participle (-ing). It shows an action in progress at a reference time. Children meet the present and past progressive in England from Year 2 (is drumming, was shouting), and the US Common Core (L.4.1b) asks Grade 4 pupils to form and use the past, present and future progressive. The future progressive is will be + -ing.

Three uses matter most at this age. The present progressive is for what is happening now (the baby is sleeping); the simple present is for habits and facts (owls hunt at night, water boils at 100 °C). The past progressive gives a background action that a shorter event in the simple past interrupts (we were walking home when it started to rain). The future progressive is for an action that will be in progress at a set time (at noon on Saturday we will be flying).

Common mistakes: leaving out be (she playing); using will without be (I will travelling); was with a plural subject (they was); the -ing form after be but no -ing (she is play); and progressive forms of state verbs such as know, want and like (I am knowing). Careful with spelling: double the final consonant after one short vowel (run → running, sit → sitting), drop a final e (make → making, write → writing, not writting), and keep y (play → playing).

In the lab your child drags the helper for six sentences shown on a past–now–future timeline, picks the right -ing spelling for six verbs and sorts six sentences into going on now or habit. Then they put the long action and the quick event on a timeline five times and fix five verb slips.

practice.prompt: At 8 last night, they ___ watching a film. Which helper fits?
practice.hint: Last night is in the past. They means more than one.
practice.explain: Past and more than one: they were watching. Was is for one person or thing; are is for now.

practice.prompt: A story has {s} sentences. {p} of them use the past progressive, like 'was running'. How many do not?
practice.hint: Take the progressive sentences away from all the sentences.
practice.explain: {s} − {p} = {=s-p} sentences do not use the past progressive.

practice.prompt: How do you spell swim + ing?
practice.hint: swim has a short i and then one m.
practice.explain: A short vowel then one consonant: double it. swim → swimming.

practice.prompt: Leo was reading for {r} minutes when the phone rang. He went on reading for {m} more minutes. How long was he reading in all?
practice.hint: Add the time before the phone rang to the time after.
practice.explain: {r} + {m} = {=r+m} minutes of reading. The reading was the long action; the ring was quick.

practice.prompt: Which sentence is about a habit?
choices: We walk to school every day.
practice.hint: Look for every day and for a verb with no -ing.
practice.explain: walk with no helper and no -ing, plus every day, shows a habit. The other two show an action going on.

pool.prompt: Tomorrow at 9, I ___ sitting my test.
pool.hint: Tomorrow is in the future, and the action will be going on.
pool.explain: The future progressive is will be + -ing: I will be sitting my test.

pool.hint: write ends in e and has a long i.
pool.explain: Drop the e and do not double the t: write → writing.

pool.prompt: 'She was reading when the phone rang.' Which action was the long one?
pool.explain: was reading was going on; rang is a quick event that cut into it.
They is more than one, so it takes were: they were playing.

pool.prompt: From 2 pm to {e} pm, Ava was painting. For how many hours was she painting?
pool.hint: Count the hours from 2 pm to the end time.
pool.explain: {e} − 2 = {=e-2} hours of painting. She was painting the whole time, so we can say 'At 3 pm she was painting'.

pool.hint: Is knowing an action you do, or a state you are in?
pool.explain: know is a state verb, so it does not usually take -ing: I know the answer.

pool.prompt: Look! The dogs ___ in the mud.
pool.hint: Look! tells you it is going on now.
pool.explain: Going on now, more than one: are + -ing. are rolling.

pool.prompt: Which verb is the past progressive?
pool.hint: Past progressive is was or were + -ing.
pool.explain: was shouting is past progressive. shouted is simple past; is shouting is present progressive.

pool.prompt: Max was walking home for {w} minutes. It started to rain {r} minutes before he got home. For how many minutes was he walking before the rain started?
pool.hint: Take the minutes in the rain away from the whole walk.
pool.explain: {w} − {r} = {=w-r} minutes. He was walking home when the rain started.
